What did eight people at Google actually invent?

one thing after another. And why the best method at the time had a crippling flaw. That's the core challenge. Sequence, order, and long-distance connections. Okay, so how did people handle that before this paper? What was the state of the art in say 2016? The dominant tool was something called a recurrent neural network.

A recurrent net, often a particular kind with a name I'll mostly avoid, but the idea is what matters. It processes a sentence the way you might read aloud. One word at a time, left to right, while maintaining a kind of running mental summary, a memory that it updates with each new word. So it reads the, updates its memory. When it reaches the end, that accumulated memory represents the whole sentence. It's an intuitive design. It mimics reading in order, and it worked reasonably well. But it had two deep problems, and this paper is essentially a frontal assault on both.

Lay out the two problems. Problem one is about memory and distance. Everything the network knows about the early part of the sentence has to survive intact in that single running summary, passed hand-to-hand from each word to the next, step after step after step. And information degrades over those steps. It's like a game of telephone down the length of the sentence. By the time the network gets to,

are, at the end, the memory of keys from the beginning has been overwritten and diluted by everything in between. So long-range dependencies, exactly the hard, important case, are exactly where these networks struggle most. The further apart two related words are, the more steps their connection has to survive, and the weaker it gets. That's the keys are problem. What's problem two?

Problem two is, in the long run, even more consequential. And it's about speed, specifically about parallelism. Because the network reads strictly in order, and each step depends on the memory from the step before, you cannot do the steps out of order or at the same time. You cannot start processing word five until you've finished words one through four, because word five needs the running memory that words one through four produced.

The computation is inherently sequential, a chain, each link waiting on the last. And that matters enormously because the hardware that powers modern AI, graphics chips, GPUs, is built to do thousands of calculations simultaneously in parallel. A sequential algorithm can't use that power. It's like having a thousand lane highway and being forced to drive single file.

So these networks were slow to train, and worse, they were slow in a way that got punishing as you tried to make them bigger and feed them more data. The sequential nature was a wall. So, you've got a method that forgets across long distances and can't be sped up by parallel hardware. And I'm guessing attention is the fix for at least one of those. Where does the word come from?

let the network, at each moment, look back at all the words of the input directly and decide which ones are relevant right now.
